A fit gives the best parameters; the profile likelihood tells how well the data determine each of
them. It is the standard tool for confidence intervals of ODE models and for practical
identifiability (Raue et al. 2009, Bioinformatics 25:1923), because it follows the objective itself
rather than its quadratic approximation at the optimum. With the symmetries of
[chapter 2](guide-symmetries.html) removed, what the profiles find is what the data, not the
equations, leave undetermined. This chapter profiles all parameters of the full model at the best
fit of [chapter 4](guide-optimization.html), takes the limits that the profiles point to, and
arrives at a reduced model whose parameters are all determined. The code is `profiles.R`.

## Profile

The profile of a parameter $\theta_i$ is the objective minimised over all other parameters with
$\theta_i$ held at a value $c$:

$$\mathrm{PL}_i(c) = \min_{\theta \,:\, \theta_i = c} \; -2 \log L(\theta) .$$

By the likelihood ratio test, the values $c$ with $\mathrm{PL}_i(c) - \mathrm{PL}_i(\hat\theta_i)$
below the $1 - \alpha$ quantile of $\chi^2_1$ form a confidence interval of level $1 - \alpha$: 3.84
for 95 %. The interval holds asymptotically, for many data points; it needs no quadratic
approximation of the objective, and it is invariant under a reparametrisation of $\theta_i$: on the
log scale it is the log of the interval on the linear scale. `profileThreshold()` computes the
threshold, and with `method = "F"` the finite-sample threshold for estimated standard deviations.

With a prior, the objective is $-2 \log$ of the posterior, and its profile mixes the data and the
prior. A question of identifiability is a question about the data alone, and so is every reduction
that follows from it. Two measures keep the prior out. First, the prior is widened before the
profiles: the weak prior of [chapter 1](guide-model.html#objective), standard deviation 4, helps the
multistart by keeping undetermined parameters finite, but it also pulls them towards its mean and so
shapes the profiles. With standard deviation 10 it still keeps the objective bounded, and its
curvature, $2/10^2 = 0.02$ per squared log unit, is small against that of the data wherever they
determine a parameter. The best fit is refitted with the wide prior, and the profiles start from
there. Second, the profiles are read through the data term,

$$\mathrm{PL}^\mathrm{data}_i(c) = -2 \log L\bigl(\hat\theta(c)\bigr),$$

with $\hat\theta(c)$ the minimiser at $\theta_i = c$, and `stepControl = list(stop = "data")`
stops a profile where the data term, not the posterior, crosses the threshold. Three shapes of it
matter:

- It rises above the threshold on both sides: the data determine $\theta_i$, and the interval is
  finite.
- It stays below the threshold on one side as far as the profile goes: the data bound $\theta_i$
  on one side only. The parameter is *practically non-identifiable*: more or other data could
  determine it, but these do not.
- It is exactly flat: a structural non-identifiability, which [chapter 2](guide-symmetries.html)
  finds from the equations and the gauge has removed.

A one-sided profile that runs to $-\infty$ on the log scale means that the process can be
switched off without a worse fit: a rate constant of 0 removes its reaction. One that runs to
$+\infty$ means that the process can be arbitrarily fast: it is in equilibrium on the time scale of
the data, and a large fixed value, or the quasi-steady state, describes it. Taking these limits
gives a smaller model with the same fit, whose remaining parameters the data can determine
(Maiwald et al. 2016, IET Syst Biol 10:76).

## Methods

Computing $\mathrm{PL}_i$ point by point is a sequence of constrained fits, each starting from the
last point.

- `method = "optimize"` moves $\theta_i$ by a step and fits all other parameters again with
  `trust()`. Every point is a converged fit, and every step costs one.
- `method = "integrate"` follows the constrained optimum as a curve. With the Lagrangian
  $f(\theta) + \lambda\,(\theta_i - c)$, the optimum satisfies $\nabla f + \lambda e_i = 0$ and
  $\theta_i = c$; differentiating with respect to $c$ gives the path equation

  $$\begin{pmatrix} H & e_i \\ e_i^\top & 0 \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{d}\theta/\mathrm{d}c \\ \mathrm{d}\lambda/\mathrm{d}c \end{pmatrix}
    = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

  with the Hessian $H$. One step needs one evaluation and one linear solve. With the Gauss-Newton
  Hessian the path drifts off the profile; `algoControl = list(reoptimize = TRUE)` corrects every
  step by a fit of the other parameters, started on the path, which needs few iterations.

Both adapt the step: the predicted change of the objective is compared with the actual one, and a
mismatch above `atol` shrinks the step, and one below `0.3 * atol`, or below `0.3 * rtol` relative
to the actual change, doubles it.

| entry of `stepControl` | `"integrate"` | `"optimize"` | controls |
|---|---|---|---|
| `stepsize` | `1e-4` | `1e-2` | first step in the profiled parameter |
| `min`, `max` | `1e-4`, `Inf` | `1e-4`, `Inf` | bounds of the step |
| `atol` | `1e-2` | `1e-1` | mismatch of predicted and actual change that rejects a step |
| `rtol` | `1e-2` | `1e-1` | relative mismatch below which the step grows |
| `limit` | `500` | `100` | steps per side |
| `stop` | `"value"` | `"value"` | the part of the objective compared with the threshold |

The correction is a `trust()` fit with the settings of `optControl`. Its tolerances have the same
meaning as in [chapter 4](guide-optimization.html) and lie above the error of the solver for the
same reason; `profiles.R` passes the `tolerances` of `model.R`. The mismatch `atol = 1e-2` that
decides a step lies four orders of magnitude above the error of the value that
[chapter 1](guide-model.html#solver-error) measures. `iterlim` bounds the iterations of one
correction. `limits` bounds the profiled parameter relative to the optimum, `side` profiles one side
only, and `cores` profiles several parameters in parallel processes.

## All parameters

`profiles.R` widens the prior and refits:

```{r wideprior, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = profiled}
# translation and degradation of A20 at the final refit against the best fit of the multistart
a20 <- c("build_A20", "degrad_A20")
a20Slower <- exp(mean(as.numeric(as.parvec(readRDS("results/fits.rds"))[a20]) -
                      readRDS("results/profiles.rds")$refit$argument[a20]))
```

It then profiles every parameter with the integration and corrections of up to 100 iterations, each
side until the data term has risen by the threshold or the parameter has moved by 7, a factor of
$e^7 \approx 1100$. A profile that reaches a lower value than its start has found a better optimum;
`profiles.R` refits from the lowest point and profiles again. Here the first pass found one: at the
better optimum, translation and degradation of A20 are both about
`r ifStored(profiled, inWords(signif(a20Slower, 1)))`fold slower, which keeps the level of A20 and
slows its turnover, and its transcript moves faster through the two delay stages.

```{r profiles, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !profiled}
cat("> Results pending: `results/profiles.rds` of the project is written by `profiles.R`.\n")
```

```{r, eval = profiled}
saved <- readRDS("results/profiles.rds")
refit <- saved$refit
profiles <- saved$profiles
objWide <- normL2(data, prd, e) + constraintL2(mu, sigma = 10)
wide <- objWide(refit$argument, fixed = gauge)
c(data = attr(wide, "data"), prior = attr(wide, "prior"))
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = profiled}
narrow <- obj(as.parvec(readRDS("results/fits.rds")), fixed = gauge)
dataDrop <- attr(narrow, "data") - attr(wide, "data")
```

With the wide prior the data term falls by about `r ifStored(profiled, round(dataDrop, 1))` below
that of the multistart: the weak prior had held some parameters away from where the data put them,
and the prior term is now small. No point of the profiles lies lower than the refit:

```{r, eval = profiled}
c(refit = refit$value, lowest = min(profiles$value))
```

The intervals from the data term, and how each profile ends:

```{r, eval = profiled}
intervals <- confint(profiles, level = 0.95, val.column = "data")
intervals$shape <- with(intervals, ifelse(is.finite(lower) & is.finite(upper), "finite",
                       ifelse(is.finite(lower), "open above",
                              ifelse(is.finite(upper), "open below", "open on both sides"))))
table(intervals$shape)
rownames(intervals) <- NULL
intervals[intervals$shape != "finite", c("name", "value", "lower", "upper", "shape")]
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = profiled}
# the largest rise of the prior on an open side, against its value at the optimum
along <- as.data.frame(profiles)
openSides <- intervals[intervals$shape != "finite", ]
priorRise <- max(mapply(function(name, shape) {
  d <- along[along$whichPar == name, ]
  side <- switch(shape, "open above" = d$constraint >= 0, "open below" = d$constraint <= 0, TRUE)
  max(d$prior[side] - d$prior[which.min(abs(d$constraint))])
}, openSides$name, openSides$shape))
```

`plotProfile()` draws the data term and the prior separately, each relative to its value at the
optimum. On an open side the data term stays below the threshold of 3.84 up to the end of the
range; what rises there is the prior, by up to `r ifStored(profiled, ceiling(10 * priorRise) / 10)`:

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 13, eval = profiled}
open <- intervals$name[intervals$shape != "finite"]
plotProfile(profiles, mode %in% c("data", "prior"), name %in% open, ncol = 4) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 3)) +
  ggplot2::theme(strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 9)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "log value", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL)
```

## Compensation

Along a profile the other parameters move to compensate the profiled one. Parameters that move
together along a flat profile form the combination the data determine. `plotPaths()` shows them.
The basal phosphorylation of IκBα, `act_Ikb_Base`, falls along its profile while the factor
`eta_act_Ikb_Base_c_pNfkIkb` rises by the same amount: the data determine the product, the rate of
IκBα phosphorylation in the complex with pNFκB, and not how much of it is basal phosphorylation of
the free complex. The import of free NFκB, `int_Nfk`, trades in the same way against the factors
of the import of IκBα and pNFκB:

```{r, fig.height = 4, eval = profiled}
plotPaths(profiles, whichPar = "act_Ikb_Base")
plotPaths(profiles, whichPar = "int_Nfk")
```

## Reduction

Each open profile proposes a limit: a rate free to go to 0 removes its process, one free to grow
without bound makes its process instantaneous, a readout parameter at 0 drops its term. Taken
together, the limits must still describe the data. The data term decides, not the prior: the
reduced model is fitted with the wide prior, and its data term is compared with that of the full
model by the likelihood ratio test, with the number of removed parameters as the degrees of
freedom. The limits of `reduced.R`, with the profile of each in the full model:

| process | parameter | profile | limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| decay of the ligand | `degrad_L` | open above | instantaneous: no ligand |
| basal activation of IKK | `act_Ikk_Base` | open below | removed |
| basal phosphorylation of NFκB | `act_Nfk_Base`, with `eta_act_Nfk_Base_c_NfkpIkb`, which only multiplies it | open below, open on both sides | removed |
| phosphorylation by ppIKK | `eta_s_ppIkk` | open above | removed |
| phosphorylation of IκBα by pIKK in the complex with pNFκB | `eta_act_Ikb_c_pNfkIkb` | open below | removed |
| inhibition of IKK by A20 | `inh_Ikk` | open on both sides | removed |
| deactivation of the receptor | `deact_TNFR` | finite | removed |
| export of the nuclear complex, its formation, degradation of pIκBα | `ext_nNfkIkb`, `eta_form_complex_nuc`, `degrad_Ikb` | open above | fast, 1000 per minute |
| release of pNFκB from the complex with pIκBα | `eta_split_pNfkpIkb` | open above | fast, 1000 per minute |
| offsets of the IκBα and pIκBα blots | `off_IkBa`, `off_ipIkBa_ibIkBa`, `off_pIkBa`, `off_ipNFkB_ibpIkBa` | open below | 0 |
| bleaching of A20-GFP | `tau_A20GFP` | open below | 0 |
| scale of the NFκB blot after NFκB precipitation | `s_ipNFkB_ibNFkB` | open below | 0, the readout is its offset |
| offset of the A20 imaging readout | `off_A20GFP` | open below | 0 |

The ligand goes with its decay: one that decays at once never reaches the receptor. The constant
of the saturation, `K_R`, is 0 by the gauge of [chapter 2](guide-symmetries.html), so without the
ligand the receptor is activated linearly in TNFα, as in the publication. Two limits are not what
a single profile proposes: the deactivation of the receptor has a finite interval, and the
phosphorylation by ppIKK is open above, not below. Both are limits of the published model
[@oppelt2018model], and the test takes them together with the others.

The other open profiles propose limits the reduced model does not take, and each of their
parameters has a finite interval in the reduced model below. Without basal phosphorylation of
IκBα, `act_Ikb_Base`, the resting cells hold no pIκBα, and together with the other limits the fit
loses more than the threshold allows; without import of free NFκB, `int_Nfk`, the IκBα of the
resting cells is degraded completely and the measured IκBα cannot be described. The activation of
IKK by the receptor, `act_Ikk_by_TNF`, moves together with the constant of its inhibition by A20
along its profile; with the inhibition removed it is left to the data. Where a limit removes a
process, `reduced.R` writes the reaction network anew; the fast rates and the vanishing readout
parameters are fixed in the transformation:

```{r reducedreactions, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r reducedobservables, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r reducedmodel, eval = FALSE}
```

The objective of the reduced model has the wide prior:

```{r reducedobjective, eval = FALSE}
```

fit, and compares the data terms:

cat("> Results pending: `results/reduced.rds` of the project is written by `refit.R`.\n")

```{r, eval = reduced}
saved <- readRDS("results/reduced.rds")
saved$ratio
```

The reduced model has `r if (reduced) round(saved$ratio[["removed"]]) else 19` fewer parameters
and a data term higher by `r if (reduced) signif(saved$ratio[["difference"]], 2) else "?"`, well below
the threshold of `r if (reduced) signif(saved$ratio[["threshold"]], 3) else "?"`: the data do not
distinguish it from the full model.

## Reduced model

`refit.R` profiles every parameter of the reduced model with the settings of `profiles.R`:

```{r reducedprofiles, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, eval = reduced}
intervalsReduced <- confint(saved$profiles, level = 0.95, val.column = "data")
intervalsReduced$shape <- with(intervalsReduced, ifelse(is.finite(lower) & is.finite(upper), "finite",
                              ifelse(is.finite(lower), "open above",
                                     ifelse(is.finite(upper), "open below", "open on both sides"))))
rownames(intervalsReduced) <- NULL
table(intervalsReduced$shape)
```

Every profile of the reduced model is finite: the data determine all of its parameters. The
intervals of the rate constants:

```{r, eval = reduced}
rates <- setdiff(intervalsReduced$name, grep("^(s|off|sigma|tau)_", intervalsReduced$name, value = TRUE))
intervalsReduced[intervalsReduced$name %in% rates, c("name", "value", "lower", "upper")]
```

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 12, eval = reduced}
plotProfile(saved$profiles, mode %in% c("data", "prior"), name %in% rates, ncol = 4) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(n = 3)) +
  ggplot2::theme(strip.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 9)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "log value", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL)
```

The publication reduced the model by the same means, profiles and the fluxes of the reactions, to a
core model of 29 reactions. The reduced model here has 29 reactions as well and agrees with it in
most limits. It differs in a few: it keeps the second delay stage of the A20 transcript and the
basal phosphorylation of IκBα, and it removes the deactivation of the receptor, which the core
model keeps at a small fixed rate.
